anchor_text: Plead my successive title with your swords
summary: 'Successive title' means the claim to inherit by right of being first-born; Saturninus argues his eldest-son standing entitles him to succeed the late emperor.
detail: Primogeniture — the eldest son's automatic right to inherit — was the standard rule of succession in both Roman and Elizabethan custom. Saturninus treats it as so obvious that an armed claim is legitimate; Bassianus, in the very next speech, counters by invoking merit and 'pure election' — which sets up the scene's central debate between hereditary title and popular choice.

anchor_text: let desert in pure election shine; And, Romans, fight for freedom in your choice
summary: Bassianus argues that the emperor should be chosen on merit ('desert') through a free popular vote, not just inherited by birth — the older Republican tradition that Marcus later enacts when he calls on the people to choose Titus.
detail: The play opens on the tension between two Roman constitutional models: hereditary imperial succession (Saturninus) and election by the Senate and people (Bassianus / Marcus). Historically, the Roman emperorship was never purely elective, but the Elizabethan reading of Rome — shaped by Livy and Plutarch — idealised the Republican assembly as the standard of free government. This opening debate shapes everything that follows: Titus hands the vote to Saturninus, bypassing both candidates, and that one decision destroys his family.

anchor_text: Chosen Andronicus, surnamed Pius
summary: 'Pius' is Latin for dutiful, pious, faithful to family and gods — the supreme Roman virtue. The cognomen (honorary second name) 'Pius' was awarded in Roman practice for outstanding public service, most famously to the emperor Antoninus Pius (ruled 138-161 CE).
detail: Roman citizens often received cognomina that recorded a personal quality or great deed: Africanus, Coriolanus, and so on. 'Pius' carries the full weight of Roman pietas — reverence toward gods, family, and country. The title is bitterly ironic by the end of the scene: Titus's 'pietas' to Rome leads him to sacrifice Tamora's son against her pleas, and to murder his own son Mutius. Shakespeare's Titus is both a perfect embodiment of Roman pietas and its victim.

anchor_text: Cometh Andronicus, bound with laurel boughs
summary: Laurel (bay) was the Roman symbol of military triumph — generals wore laurel wreaths in their triumph processions, and the emperor held a sprig of laurel when accepting a general's victory dispatch. Titus's laurel crown marks him as a triumphant general re-entering Rome.

Roman triumphatores, imperatores, and eventually emperors all used the laurel. At the same time, the laurel wreath was associated with poets — the 'laureate' — which gives Shakespeare a slight double register: Titus is both the soldier and, briefly, an elegist for his dead sons. The mixture of 'mourning weeds' and laurel boughs in the same procession captures the scene's blend of triumph and grief.

anchor_text: Half of the number that King Priam had
summary: Priam was the king of Troy who, in Greek myth, fathered fifty sons — the largest royal family of the ancient world. Titus had twenty-five sons and has lost twenty-one of them, leaving him, as he says, with 'the poor remains' of four. The comparison sets his grief within the scale of Troy's catastrophic loss.

The Trojan War is the play's persistent backdrop — Aaron will later compare himself to Simon the deceiver, Tamora to the Queen of Troy, and the fall of Titus's house is built on the fall-of-Troy archetype.

anchor_text: hover on the dreadful shore of Styx
summary: The Styx was the great river of the classical underworld that the dead had to cross to reach their final rest. Titus says his unburied sons are stranded on its near bank — shades without a grave cannot cross, so their spirits hover restlessly between the living and the dead.
detail: In Greek and Roman belief, the proper burial rite was essential: without it the soul could not board Charon's ferry across the Styx and entered the underworld in a permanent limbo. Virgil (Aeneid 6.295-330) describes the unburied dead crowding the near shore, waiting a hundred years before they can cross. This is what drives Lucius's demand for a sacrificial victim: the shades of the fallen Andronici are 'unappeas'd' until the rite is performed. The Styx shore is also the play's first use of the underworld imagery that will build through Titus's later descent.

anchor_text: O sacred receptacle of my joys, Sweet cell of virtue and nobility, How many sons of mine hast thou in store
summary: Titus addresses the tomb directly as if it were a person — a rhetorical figure called apostrophe. He calls it 'sacred receptacle' (holy container) and 'sweet cell' (room or chamber), personifying it as a keeper of both his sons and his pride. The speech intensifies the audience's sense of how much of Titus's identity is bound up in his family tomb.
detail: The apostrophe to the tomb — 'O sacred receptacle' — is modelled on the emotional addresses to temples and gods in Senecan drama. 'Receptacle' carries the full Latin sense of receptaculum, a place that receives and holds. The tomb already holds twenty-one of Titus's sons; the question 'how many ... hast thou in store?' bleakly anticipates that it will hold more. The 'sweet cell of virtue' echoes the closing 'Secure from worldly chances' speech (TLN 152-155) — the tomb is the only place in the play that does not disappoint.

anchor_text: Ad manes fratrum sacrifice his flesh Before this earthy prison of their bones
summary: Latin: 'to the shades of our brothers.' The 'manes' (pronounced mah-nays) were the collective spirits of the dead in Roman religion; Lucius proposes to hew up Alarbus as an offering to appease the shades of Titus's fallen sons gathered around their tomb.
detail: Manes is the plural noun (always treated as such in Latin) for the souls of the dead — the ancestral spirits who lived on in a collective underworld existence and could harm the living if left unhonoured. Roman state religion required propitiatory offerings at tombs, especially for the violent dead. The practice Shakespeare invents here for Lucius — burning and dismembering a prisoner to feed the fires — is closer to Homeric human sacrifice (Achilles over Patroclus's pyre, Iliad 23) than to historical Roman ritual, but it draws on a real Roman anxiety about the restless, unavenged dead.

anchor_text: shadows be not unappeas'd, Nor we disturb'd with prodigies on earth
summary: 'Shadows' here means the ghosts of the dead. Roman belief held that the spirits of the violent dead sent 'prodigies' — supernatural disturbances such as strange apparitions, blood-rain, or earthquake — to the living if they went unavenged or unburied.

Cicero's De Divinatione lists types of prodigia; Livy's histories are full of them. The logic Lucius states is precise: no sacrifice = unquiet shades = prodigies afflict Rome. This is the stated reason for Alarbus's killing, and it reflects real Roman sacrificial theology even as the specific practice is dramatically heightened.

anchor_text: Stay, Roman brethen
summary: Tamora's speech is a formal supplication (Greek proskunesis, Roman supplicatio): she invokes the gods, mirrors Titus's own feeling as a parent, appeals to piety, and ends with a direct plea. This kind of structured plea was a recognized rhetorical form in both classical oratory and Elizabethan schoolroom composition.
detail: The speech moves through four deliberate steps: (1) address and claim of shared feeling ('if thy sons were ever dear to thee'); (2) the argument from equity ('it is in these'); (3) the argument from religious duty ('draw near the nature of the gods ... in being merciful'); (4) the direct petition ('spare my first-born son'). Tamora's failed appeal is the rhetorical mirror image of the successful one she delivers later in the same scene (TLN 434ff), where she has the power to enforce her argument. Marcus's Ajax speech later in the scene (TLN 384) works the same formal structure.

anchor_text: Wilt thou draw near the nature of the gods? Draw near them, then, in being merciful
summary: Tamora argues that mercy is divine — to be merciful is to resemble the gods; to refuse it is bestial. This was a Stoic and Neo-Platonic commonplace in Renaissance ethics, familiar from Cicero and from the debate about clemency versus justice in Roman political theory.
detail: The idea that the gods are characterised by clemency (clementia) had political force: Julius Caesar used it as a governing virtue, and Seneca wrote an entire treatise, De Clementia, addressed to Nero, arguing that mercy distinguishes the king from the tyrant. Titus's rejection of Tamora's appeal signals to the audience that his rigidly Roman 'piety' has crowded out the very virtue that would have made him genuinely divine. Portia's 'quality of mercy' speech in The Merchant of Venice (c. 1596, roughly contemporary with Titus) draws on the same tradition.

anchor_text: O cruel, irreligious piety
summary: An oxymoron: 'piety' (religious duty) that is simultaneously 'irreligious.' Tamora's point is that Titus's act is a contradiction in terms — he claims to be honoring the gods of Rome through sacrifice, yet the act is itself a violation of divine mercy. The compressed paradox captures the play's central problem in five words.
detail: Oxymoron (combining contradictory terms) is a favourite device in Senecan tragic rhetoric, and this is one of the most pointed in all of Shakespeare. Tamora means that Roman pietas — duty to ancestors, family, gods — has been perverted into something that offends the gods by its cruelty. The audience will be asked throughout whether Titus's rigid adherence to Roman honour is heroic or monstrous; Tamora's phrase opens that question the moment Alarbus is taken off to be dismembered.

anchor_text: Was ever Scythia half so barbarous
summary: Scythia was the name Greeks and Romans gave to the vast steppes north of the Black Sea, and 'Scythian' was a byword in classical literature for barbarian savagery. Chiron uses it to say that Rome, supposedly the civilised power, has now out-barbarized even the most feared 'uncivilized' people the ancients knew.
detail: Herodotus (Histories 4) describes the Scythians in lurid detail — drinking from enemy skulls, scalping, making cloaks of enemy skin. They were the classical world's stock exemplar of savage nomads, as the Goths became in the late antique period. Chiron's line sets up the play's core irony: the 'barbarian' Goths repeatedly voice humane objections (mercy, burial, justice) that the Romans refuse to act on. By Act 5 it is the Romans — Chiron and Demetrius aside — who have committed the worst horrors.

anchor_text: aspir'd to Solon's happiness And triumphs over chance in honour's bed
summary: Solon, the Athenian lawgiver (c. 638-558 BCE), famously told the wealthy King Croesus that no man should be counted happy until he is dead — because fortune can reverse even at the last moment. Marcus is saying that the soldiers who died in their country's service achieved 'Solon's happiness': they are safely dead in honour and cannot be robbed of it by the turns of Fortune.
detail: Herodotus (Histories 1.29-33) tells the story: the fabulously rich Croesus asked Solon who was the happiest man he had seen; Solon named an obscure Athenian who died gloriously in battle, not Croesus. He explained that Fortune overturns the great — 'call no man happy till he is dead' (Greek: meden praxis makarizon). The phrase passed into proverbial wisdom across Europe. Marcus applies it to the fallen Andronici: they have reached a state of happiness that Fortune can no longer touch. The irony is that Titus — the survivor — is about to be ground into misery by exactly the Fortune Solon warned about.

anchor_text: This palliament of white and spotless hue; And name thee in election for the empire
summary: A 'palliament' is a robe; the specific 'white and spotless' robe is the toga candida — the brilliant white toga that Roman candidates for office wore when seeking votes, which is the origin of our word 'candidate' (from Latin candidus, white).
detail: Roman candidates at elections whitened their togas with chalk (creta) to make them visible in the crowds and to signal purity of intention. Marcus then uses the technical term: 'Be candidatus then, and put it on' (TLN 185) — a 'candidatus' was literally a white-robed man. The word candidate entered English via this tradition. The white toga is a visual emblem: whoever puts it on claims to be worthy of power on grounds of personal virtue. Titus refuses it, which sets the whole crisis in motion.

anchor_text: I ask your voices and your suffrages
summary: 'Voices' and 'suffrages' both mean votes. A 'suffrage' (Latin suffragium) was a ballot or vote in Roman assemblies; 'voices' was the common Elizabethan equivalent for public acclamation. Titus is asking the tribunes and people to cast their votes.

The doubling here ('voices and suffrages') may reflect the assembly's two stages: public acclamation followed by formal vote. Titus's move to ask the crowd to ratify the choice removes the decision from the patricians alone and grounds it in popular sovereignty — the same move Marcus used to convene the election — which makes Titus's subsequent gift of the empire to Saturninus all the more politically consequential.

The allusion is darkly ironic — Dido was abandoned by Aeneas and killed herself; Tamora, who invites the Dido parallel, is herself about to unleash catastrophe. anchor_text: Venus govern your desires, Saturn is dominator over mine

anchor_text: His Philomel must lose her tongue to-day
summary: Aaron calls Lavinia 'his Philomel' — a direct reference to the myth of Philomela, the Athenian princess raped by King Tereus, who then cut out her tongue so she could not name him. This myth structures the entire play: Lavinia is Philomela (raped and silenced), Titus is Procne (the avenger who kills the rapists' 'children' — in his case, Chiron and Demetrius themselves — and serves them to their mother). Aaron's use of the name 'Philomel' as a code-name for Lavinia is the play's first explicit identification of the mythic parallel, preparing audiences for every subsequent Ovidian reference. Arthur Golding's English translation (1567) was Shakespeare's direct source.

anchor_text: Thy temples should be planted presently With horns, as was Actaeon's
summary: Tamora threatens Bassianus with the fate of Actaeon, a hunter who stumbled upon Diana bathing in her sacred pool; the goddess punished his intrusion by turning him into a stag, after which his own hounds tore him apart. Tamora casts herself as the wronged Diana and Bassianus as the impertinent trespasser who deserves to be hunted down.

Shakespeare's play voices this racism through its Roman characters while simultaneously giving Aaron intelligence, selfhood, and parental love that complicate the stereotype. anchor_text: A barren detested vale you see it is: The trees, though summer, yet forlorn and lean, O'ercome with moss and baleful mistletoe

'Baleful mistletoe' draws on mistletoe's associations with death and druidic magic (it grows on oaks without touching the soil, as if supernatural); 'urchins' at TLN 772 means hedgehogs, associated in folklore with witchcraft and malevolence. Lavinia deploys the name at the moment Bassianus's body is still warm and Tamora's sons are about to drag her off — its force is that it names the very worst comparator Lavinia can summon, and then withdraws it as still insufficient. 'Thrash the corn' separates grain from husk through violent beating — the metaphor reduces Lavinia to a raw material and her rape to an agricultural process. 'Minion' in this context is contemptuous: a creature who 'stands upon' (insists on, makes much of) her chastity as if it were a bargaining chip she can deploy against her betters. anchor_text: Therefore away with her, and use her as you will; The worse to her the better lov'd of me
summary: This couplet functions as a stage direction in dialogue: Tamora explicitly authorizes rape as an act of loyalty to herself. 'Use her as you will' gives Chiron and Demetrius permission to do whatever they choose with Lavinia; 'the worse to her the better lov'd of me' makes cruelty toward Lavinia a measure of their devotion to their mother. Tamora then exits, leaving the assault to happen off stage.
detail: The line is remarkable for its directness — Tamora neither softens nor equivocates the instruction. The grammar is causative: the superlative 'the worse... the better' is a rhetorical figure (correlative comparison) that makes Lavinia's suffering the currency in which her sons pay their love to Tamora. That Tamora then exits means the audience never sees the assault: it takes place off stage, and Lavinia returns in the next scene tongueless and handless. The convention of off-stage atrocity is Senecan in origin — Seneca's tragedies report horror rather than staging it — though the subsequent visible entry of the mutilated Lavinia is among the most viscerally confronting stage moments in the Elizabethan repertoire.

anchor_text: 'Tis present death I beg; and one thing more, That womanhood denies my tongue to tell

anchor_text: go tell, an if thy tongue can speak
summary: Demetrius and Chiron speak in sustained cruel irony: they tell Lavinia to 'go tell' who attacked her, knowing they have cut out her tongue; they invite her to 'write down thy mind,' knowing they have cut off her hands. By issuing commands that cannot be obeyed, Chiron and Demetrius act out the logic of the crime itself: they have engineered not only physical destruction but the total suppression of testimony. Marcus later supplies the structural term when he names Philomela: the rapists have pre-emptively silenced the witness. The grim wit here is Senecan in tone — the villains savour their own cleverness — and sets up the play's central dramatic problem: how does a woman with no tongue and no hands name her attackers?

anchor_text: Hear me, grave fathers! noble tribunes, stay
summary: Titus addresses the senators as 'grave fathers,' the Latin phrasing of 'patres' by which Roman senators were formally addressed — stressing their rank as the patriarchal guardians of Rome. The senators' silent exit while Titus prostrates himself enacts the play's central crisis: Rome has stopped being governed by the traditional bonds of pietas (duty, piety, family loyalty). The image of a general who sacrificed twenty-two sons begging in the dust for the lives of two more is deliberately extreme — and the tribunes' stony departure amplifies the pathos by refusing any response.

summary: 'Mesh'd' (meshed, strained through a mesh or sieve) is a brewing term: when making ale, the brewer 'mashed' the malt by steeping and straining it. anchor_text: What dost thou strike at, Marcus, with thy knife
summary: The 'fly scene' — in which Titus first condemns Marcus as a murderer for killing a harmless fly, then reverses himself when Marcus calls the fly black 'like to the empress' Moor' — is the scene's emotional and structural center. His plan to raise the boy on 'berries and on roots,' curds and whey, and goat's milk, and to bring him up 'to be a warrior' follows a pastoral exile pattern familiar from romance — but Aaron's version of it is practical military training, not pastoral idyll. 'As swift as swallow flies' is a simile from nature, the swallow being the type of speed.

anchor_text: Terras Astrea reliquit
summary: 'Terras Astraea reliquit' is Latin for 'Astraea has left the earth.' Astraea was the goddess of justice who, in classical myth, abandoned the wicked world of men and was transformed into the constellation Virgo. Titus cries the line as he hunts for Justice among the gods, meaning justice no longer exists on earth.
detail: The line is adapted from Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.149-150 (in Golding's 1567 English: 'The virgin Astraea last of all the heavenly wights did leave the slaughter-stained earth'). Ovid places her departure at the end of the Iron Age, when human wickedness had reached its worst. Titus's allusion is exact and bitter: he is living in an iron world where courts dispense cruelty, not law, and the only recourse is to seek a goddess who has already fled. The same figure appears in 1 Henry VI, where Astraea's return is used as a symbol of golden-age renewal — here the emphasis falls on her absence. Her identification with Virgo also primes the astronomical wordplay that follows when the shooting arrows are said to reach 'in Virgo's lap' (TLN 1803).

anchor_text: Pierce the inmost centre of the earth: Then, when you come to Pluto's region
summary: Pluto was the Roman god of the dead, who ruled the underworld beneath the earth. Titus sends his kinsmen to dig down to Pluto's realm with a petition for justice, since he cannot find it anywhere on the surface of the world. The joke — digging to hell to file a legal complaint — shows Titus's anguished absurdity.
detail: In classical cosmology the underworld (variously called Hades, Tartarus, Orcus, or Pluto's realm) lay beneath the earth; souls reached it by crossing rivers such as the Styx and Acheron. Titus proceeds systematically — he will look for Justice in the sea (cousins with nets), underground (Publius and Sempronius with mattock and spade), and finally in the sky (arrows shot at the gods). Virgil, Aeneid 6, describes the geography of the underworld in detail; Seneca's tragedies (the primary influence on this play) are full of appeals to Pluto and the infernal powers. The scene's dark comedy turns on the Roman theatrical convention that Hades was below the stage trap.

anchor_text: burning lake below, And pull her out of Acheron by the heels
summary: Acheron was one of the rivers of the classical underworld, sometimes described as a burning or black lake rather than a flowing river. Titus threatens to dive in and drag Justice out bodily if Pluto will not send her up. The defiant image is characteristically Senecan — the hero who would wrestle death itself rather than endure injustice.
detail: Acheron (Greek 'river of woe') is named by Virgil in Aeneid 6 among the rivers Aeneas must cross; Seneca uses the word freely as a general term for the underworld in his tragedies. The 'burning lake' may conflate Acheron with the fiery river Phlegethon, or simply reflect a popular conception of hell-fire. Titus's vow to drag Justice 'by the heels' is comic in its physicality, suggesting he would treat the abstract personification as a struggling prisoner. Seneca's Thyestes, a key source for the play's revenge banquet, is full of exactly this rhetoric of defying the gods and the underworld.

anchor_text: in Virgo's lap
summary: Virgo is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, pictured as a seated woman; a shot landing 'in Virgo's lap' means it flew so high it reached the stars. The joke doubles on the name: Astraea, the goddess of Justice Titus is hunting, was identified with the constellation Virgo (Titus cited that at TLN 1742). So landing in Virgo's lap is nearly arriving at Justice herself.
detail: The wordplay binds the scene's astronomical comedy to its serious theme. Titus opened this scene crying 'Terras Astraea reliquit' — Justice/Astraea has fled to the heavens as Virgo. Marcus's quip that the arrow landed 'in Virgo's lap' is therefore not merely a joke about altitude; it brings the whole wild enterprise of shooting petitions into the sky close to something like success — the arrow actually reached the zodiac sign under which Justice sits. The double meaning was readily available to any grammar-school reader who knew both Ovid's cosmological mythology and the zodiac.

anchor_text: Marcus, the post is come
summary: A 'post' was a courier or messenger, especially one who travelled between fixed relay stations (each called a 'post') along a road, changing horses as he went. Titus mistakes the Clown for a divine messenger arriving from heaven with an answer to his arrows — a delusion that drives the scene's comedy.

anchor_text: going with my pigeons to the tribunal plebs, to take up a matter of brawl betwixt my uncle
summary: The Clown mangles 'tribunal plebis' — the court of the tribunes of the people, a Roman legal assembly where commoners brought disputes. The garbled Latin is part of his characterisation as an ordinary man out of his depth in a world of soldiers and senators; he is going, in his own terms, to the local magistrate to settle a neighbourhood fight.
detail: The tribuni plebis (tribunes of the plebs) were elected Roman magistrates whose function was to protect common citizens against patrician power; their court, the tribunal plebis, heard civil disputes. Shakespeare uses the malapropism to comic effect: the Clown's version shows that he half-knows there is a Latin name for the place without knowing what it means. It also plants a structural irony — the Clown is headed to one legal court (to settle his uncle's brawl), while Titus redirects him to another (the imperial court), and the mixing of the two courts will prove fatal to the Clown, who is hanged for delivering Titus's defiant message.

anchor_text: can you deliver an oration to the emperor with a grace? Nay, truly, sir, I could never say grace in all my life.
summary: Titus uses 'grace' to mean the dignified manner in which an oration is delivered — rhetorical grace, elegance of bearing. The Clown hears only the word's everyday domestic sense: saying grace before a meal, a simple religious routine he has presumably never managed. The exchange is one of the scene's moments of genuine comedy inside the surrounding violence.

anchor_text: was ever seen An emperor in Rome thus overborne
summary: 'Overborne' means overwhelmed, defeated, or subdued by superior force. Saturninus is asking whether a Roman emperor has ever been so humiliated and defied — the irony being that the arrows Titus shot into the sky, addressed to the gods, have been read as a public accusation against him.

'Extent of legal justice' (line 1857-58) means the exercise or enforcement of legal punishment. Saturninus's opening complaint establishes him as a tyrant masking injustice in legal language — the sons of Titus whom he executed were, he insists, lawfully condemned, not 'butchered wrongfully.'

anchor_text: here's to Jove, and this to Mercury; This to Apollo; this to the God of War
summary: Titus has shot arrows into the sky with messages attached, each addressed to a Roman deity: Jove (Jupiter, king of the gods and god of justice), Mercury (divine messenger), Apollo (god of justice and truth), and Mars (god of war). Titus is petitioning heaven itself for redress because earthly justice has failed him — a mad, spectacular act that terrifies Saturninus precisely because the people of Rome can read it as a public shaming.
detail: The selection of gods is not random. Jupiter and Apollo were associated with justice and divine order; Mercury, as messenger of the gods, was the appropriate carrier of petitions to heaven; Mars was invoked because Titus himself is a soldier of Rome. Seneca's tragedies frequently staged heroes addressing the gods from extreme desperation, and this scene draws on that tradition. Saturninus's panic — 'blazoning our injustice everywhere' — reveals the arrows have worked: the gods, and Rome's citizens, are now witnesses.

anchor_text: libelling against the senate, And blazoning our injustice everywhere
summary: 'Libelling' meant publishing false or defamatory accusations — a serious legal offense. 'Blazoning' means proclaiming or displaying openly, often publicly posting a charge. Saturninus reads Titus's arrow-messages as both a crime (libel against the state) and a public humiliation, broadcasting to all of Rome that its emperor is unjust.
detail: In Elizabethan England, publishing libels against rulers or magistrates was a punishable offense; the Elizabethan Star Chamber prosecuted libels vigorously. 'Blaze abroad' was a common idiom for making something widely and humiliatingly public. Saturninus's response — fear, fury, a desire to silence Titus — shows that the accusation has hit home. The irony Shakespeare builds is that Saturninus's guilt makes him read the arrows as a true indictment even though he insists everything was done 'with law.'

anchor_text: feigned ecstasies Shall be no shelter to these outrages
summary: 'Ecstasies' here does not mean joy; it is the Elizabethan word for fits of madness or mental derangement — the condition of being 'beside oneself.' Saturninus believes Titus is faking this madness as a legal shield: if Titus can claim lunacy, he cannot be prosecuted for his provocations. The threat is that Saturninus will punish him anyway.
detail: The Greek root ek-stasis means 'standing outside oneself,' and the word covered everything from prophetic trance to violent fits. Hamlet also uses 'ecstasy' for madness. The political point is sharp: in Roman law, as in English common law, a madman could not be held criminally responsible for his acts. Whether Titus's madness is feigned or real is a question the play keeps open; Saturninus's reading — that it is strategic — is not without basis.

anchor_text: High-witted Tamora to gloze with all
summary: In an aside addressed to herself, Tamora celebrates her own cleverness: 'high-witted' means sharp-minded, crafty. 'Gloze' means to smooth things over with flattery and deception — to gloss a bad situation with pleasing words. Tamora congratulates herself on performing false sympathy for Titus in front of Saturninus while actually engineering his destruction.

The word 'gloze' (related to 'gloss') carried a negative charge of dishonesty — to gloze was to use fair-seeming language to conceal a deceitful purpose. Tamora's self-praise as 'high-witted' echoes Aaron's earlier delight in his own cunning; both characters articulate their villainy as intellectual superiority, a feature of the Senecan villain Shakespeare is drawing on throughout the play.

anchor_text: God and Saint Stephen give you good-den
summary: The Clown — a rustic, comic character — blunders into the palace greeting the Empress with a folk expression from rural England: 'God and Saint Stephen give you good-den' means 'God and St Stephen give you good evening.' Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr (Acts 7), had a feast day on 26 December and was widely invoked as a popular saint in Elizabethan England. The greeting is jarring because it is entirely out of place in ancient Rome — and marks the Clown as comically ignorant of where he is.
detail: The Clown's intrusion is Shakespeare's one moment of low comedy in this very dark scene: he has been sent by Titus with a letter and a pair of pigeons to deliver to the emperor, but he cannot tell Tamora from the emperor. His homely English oath — invoking a Christian saint in a pagan Roman court — is anachronistic nonsense, and the play does not try to explain it. The Clown's cheerful incomprehension of his danger (he asks how much money he will be paid, even as Saturninus orders him hanged) makes his death both absurd and tragic — an innocent destroyed by power he cannot understand.

anchor_text: I have brought up a neck to a fair end
summary: Told he will be hanged, the Clown cracks a grim joke: 'I have brought up a neck to a fair end.' 'Brought up' means both raised from childhood (as one raises a child) and now applied literally — his neck has been raised to its fitting conclusion: the noose. It is black comedy. The Clown treats his own execution as the natural completion of his errand, not understanding or not caring about his death.
detail: The Clown's response to the sentence of death is one of the most unsettling moments in the play precisely because he does not react with terror. Whether this is stupidity, courage, or Shakespearean absurdism is left deliberately ambiguous. The pun on 'brought up' (reared; now led to execution) makes a joke out of a life and its end — a kind of dark play on the neck's role in hanging. Critics sometimes read this as Shakespeare's signal that the world of Titus is so saturated with violence that even innocents absorb it as routine.

anchor_text: in course of this revenge, to do As much as ever Coriolanus did
summary: Aemilius reports that Lucius, Titus's banished son, now leads the Gothic army against Rome 'as much as ever Coriolanus did.' Coriolanus was a legendary Roman hero who, banished from Rome, turned against his own city and led an enemy army to its walls — only to be talked out of the final assault by his mother's appeal. The comparison is a direct threat: Lucius is doing what Coriolanus did, and Rome should be afraid.
detail: The Coriolanus comparison is the play's only explicit invocation of this earlier Roman legend, and it is historically precise. Gaius Marcius Coriolanus, according to Livy and Plutarch, was a patrician general who captured the Volscian city of Corioli (winning his surname), was banished for political arrogance, and joined Rome's enemies to march on the city — stopping only when his mother Volumnia pleaded with him at the gates. In Titus the parallel underscores Lucius's claim to legitimacy: like Coriolanus, he was unjustly expelled, and like Coriolanus, he has found strength among Rome's foes. Shakespeare would later write Coriolanus as a full play (c. 1608).

The Coriolanus parallel — banished general leading enemy forces to Rome's walls, stopped by a family appeal — maps precisely onto Lucius's situation and is the mainstream reading; noting Shakespeare later wrote the full play is accurate and contextually useful without overreaching.

anchor_text: baits to fish or honey-stalks to sheep, Whenas the one is wounded with the bait, The other rotted with delicious feed
summary: Tamora boasts that her words will ensnare Titus with two parallel images: fish are caught by baits that wound them on a hidden hook, and sheep are killed by gorging on clover ('honey-stalks') — the sweet feed rots them from within (a real agricultural danger called 'bloat'). She will destroy Titus through pleasure and trust rather than force.
detail: The pair of natural-world comparisons (fish-bait, sheep-bloat) is a doublet of exempla, a favourite Elizabethan rhetorical pattern. 'Honey-stalks' are stalks of clover, which really can kill sheep if they eat too much when wet — a fact of Elizabethan husbandry well-known to a rural audience. The images tell us more than Tamora intends: both traps work by offering something desirable (food, sweetness) that conceals destruction.
